analysis_steps.goal: Extract spatially integrated [CII] spectrum and measure line properties

method.value: Iterative aperture and masking procedure following Bethermin et al. (2020): place beam-area aperture at source center, extract spectrum, fit Gaussian to get FWHM, create moment-0 map over FWHM, mask cube at >3 sigma, and repeat until spectrum converges.

evidence.quote: This is an iterative process where a small aperture equal to the area of the beam width is centred on the main source of emission ($\alpha$ = 09:59:30.459, $\delta$ = 2.08.02.586); using this aperture, an integrated spectrum is extracted and a Gaussian profile can be fitted to the emission; the full width at half maximum (FWHM) from this fit is used to create a simple moment-0 map which in turn provides a mask—by taking all emission greater than 3$\sigma$—and then masks the entire cube.
This masked cube is used to extract another integrated spectrum, and the process is repeated, until the extracted integrated spectrum remains unchanged.

analysis_steps.goal: Extract surface brightness radial profiles and fit Sersic models to [CII] and UV maps

method.value: Convolve HST images with the ALMA beam. Determine emission peaks via independent 1D Gaussian fits to RA- and Dec-summed profiles. Place concentric annuli in 0.1" bins around the peak, compute area-normalized flux and uncertainties (Eqs. 1 and 2), and fit Sersic profiles (both free n and fixed n=1) using emcee.

evidence.quote: A radial profile was generated by placing a series of increasingly larger annuli, in bins of 0.1", around the peak [CII] emission of the moment-0 map. This peak was determined by summing up the emission along the RA and Dec axis independently and then determining the central RA and Dec values which were calculated from the resulting two, independent, 1-D Gaussian fits.
A Sérsic profile was adopted in order to fit the radial profiles using a Monte-Carlo Markov-chain fitting routine, with the python package `emcee` (cite: emcee).
To appropriately compare morphologies between the HST and ALMA data, the high resolution HST data was convolved with the ALMA beam.

claims.hypothesis: Main-sequence galaxy HZ7 at z = 5.25 possesses an extended [CII] halo around its rest-frame UV star-forming core.
claims.experiment: Compared 0.27" resolution ALMA [CII] moment-0 radial profiles and 2D surface brightness distribution against ALMA-beam-convolved HST/WFC3 F105W, F125W, and F160W rest-frame UV images using MCMC Sersic profile fitting and >4 sigma halo tests.
claims.result: Measured R_e,[CII] = 3.60 (+0.49/-0.64) kpc (free n) and 3.07 (+0.23/-0.25) kpc (fixed n=1) versus average rest-frame UV R_e ~ 1.48 +/- 0.16 kpc (n=1), giving a [CII]-to-UV size ratio of 2-3 and passing >4 sigma halo criteria.
claims.finding: HZ7 shows strong direct observational evidence of an extended [CII] halo surrounding its rest-frame UV emission.

evidence.quote: For a matched Sérsic profile with n = 1, we measured a [CII] effective radius of $0.50\pm 0.04$" (3.07$\pm 0.25$ kpc) and an average rest-frame UV effective radius of $0.2\pm0.04$" ($1.48\pm0.16$ kpc).

Therefore, (cite: Herrera-Camus2021) suggest a more physical, but similar, definition: measuring if the extended [CII] emission—the emission which extends further than the rest-frame UV emission—is greater than $4\sigma$. In both definitions, HZ7 is considered a system with a [CII] halo.

claims.hypothesis: HZ7 is a merging system rather than an ordered, rotating disk galaxy, and tidal interactions/shocks or obscured emission may explain the extended [CII] emission.
claims.experiment: Constructed 3-sigma masked [CII] moment-1 (velocity field) and moment-2 (velocity dispersion) maps and compared the spatial morphology of [CII], rest-frame UV, and dust continuum.
claims.result: The moment-1 map lacks any velocity gradient and the moment-2 map is disordered; the [CII] morphology has a NE tendril and knots, dust continuum has a southern extension, and log(L_[CII]/L_FIR) > 1.5.
claims.finding: HZ7 is unequivocally not a simple rotating disk and is likely a merging system, though confirming the merger and the exact halo mechanism requires deeper follow-up observations.

evidence.quote: Both higher-order moment maps are disordered with the velocity field in the middle panel of Figure 2 showing no indication of a gradient and therefore no clear indication of a rotating disk.

The overall structure of both the moment-1 and moment-2 maps suggest that HZ7 could possibly be a merger. This is further supported by the southern continuum emission in Figure 3. Determining whether or not the system is actually a merger would require further inspection and study, including follow-up high resolution ALMA observations.

claims.hypothesis: The extended [CII] halo in HZ7 is driven by fast cooling outflows detectable as shifted or broad secondary velocity components across the galaxy.
claims.experiment: Placed seven small circular apertures (radii 0.05" and 0.02") around HZ7 following Herrera-Camus et al. (2021) and examined the extracted [CII] spectra.
claims.result: No velocity offsets or wider secondary line components were detected in the aperture spectra.
claims.finding: There is no spectral evidence for outflows in HZ7 at the sensitivity of the current ALMA observations.

evidence.quote: We checked for extended velocity components across the galaxy, which would imply the presence of an outflow, following the analysis of (cite: Herrera-Camus2021).
However, we found that there was no evidence for an outflow, which would be identified as an offset or wider secondary line components in the spectra, at the sensitivity of our observations.

why_this_data.value: HZ7 is one of the brightest normal main-sequence (near L*) galaxies in the Capak et al. (2015) z~5 sample with good multiwavelength coverage, and 0.3" ALMA observations match HST angular resolution to directly resolve [CII] vs UV morphology without stacking.

evidence.quote: In this paper we study the observations of HZ7 in particular, one of the brightest objects in the (cite: Capak2015) sample, with a rest-frame UV spectroscopic redshift of z = 5.2532±0.0004 (cite: Capak2015).
Here we present high signal-to-noise ALMA [CII] follow-up observations of HZ7 at an angular resolution comparable to that of HST and JWST.

why_this_method.value: Concatenating compact-configuration data increases sensitivity to extended emission, JvM correction fixes multi-configuration CLEAN flux scaling, HST convolution matches the ALMA PSF, and independent profile centering removes residual astrometric offsets.

evidence.quote: The previous data was taken in a more compact configuration providing extra sensitivity to extended emission.

Since the residual map which results from the CLEAN algorithm can have incorrect default flux scaling when combining different array configurations (cite: JVM1995), we apply a correction as suggested by (cite: JvMModern2021).
To appropriately compare morphologies between the HST and ALMA data, the high resolution HST data was convolved with the ALMA beam.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Outflows as the origin of the [CII] halo: tested via multi-aperture spectra but no velocity offsets or secondary broad components were found at current sensitivity.

evidence.quote: However, we found that there was no evidence for an outflow, which would be identified as an offset or wider secondary line components in the spectra, at the sensitivity of our observations.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Central dust obscuration suppressing UV emission to mimic a [CII] halo: considered unlikely because HZ7 would have to be dust-poor in the center and dust-rich in the outskirts, contrary to observations and theory.

evidence.quote: But based on these results of HZ7, the galaxy would be dust poor towards the center, which seems unlikely. There would also be an expectation for the [CII] and dust emission to be aligned, and dust emission towards the outskirts of the system. Both of these criteria are not observed in this data.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Bright in-falling satellite clumps producing the [CII] halo: no bright clumps are seen in the diffuse halo at 0.3" (~2 kpc) resolution, so any clumps would have to be numerous and much smaller than 2 kpc.

evidence.quote: However, we only find an extended diffuse emission, with no signs of bright clumps, at the resolution of our observations (0.3" $\sim$ 2 kpc). This implies that if indeed the extended emission is produced by clumps, they would have to be numerous and significantly smaller than 2 kpc.

limitations_admitted.value: It is not possible to determine the exact physical process behind the observed [CII] halo from these ALMA observations alone.

evidence.quote: In the case of HZ7, it is not possible to determine the exact physical process or processes behind the observed [CII] halo from these ALMA observations alone.

limitations_admitted.value: Current sensitivity/SNR of the observations may be insufficient to detect faint outflow components or to draw firm conclusions from the dust continuum morphology.

evidence.quote: This could imply that either deeper, or higher signal-to-noise, observations might be necessary in order to detect evidence of outflows.

It is entirely possible that the continuum data does not have a high enough SNR in order to make any firm deductions. Higher S/N observations of the continuum would be needed in order to fully investigate its contribution

referee_caveats_inferred: The 1D radial profile fitting uses circular annuli rather than elliptical annuli despite the elongated NE morphology of the [CII] emission.

The uncertainty formula for the HST annular flux, u(F) = sqrt(n*sigma^2 + F), sums background variance and source flux in raw units without explicitly stating the gain/exposure conversion to electron counts or accounting for correlated noise after convolving the HST image with the ALMA beam.

In Section 4.2.1, the lower limit on log(L_[CII]/L_FIR) is written as >1.5 based on log(L_[CII]/L_sun) = 8.8 and log(L_FIR/L_sun) < 10.35, which is actually log(L_FIR/L_[CII]) < 1.55 (or log(L_[CII]/L_FIR) > -1.55).
